source.title: Mini-Proceedings ECT* Workshop: Hadronic Atoms and Kaonic Nuclei

accepted.question_text: In low-energy antikaon-nucleon physics, is the isospin-0, orbital-angular-momentum-0 K−p quasi-bound state the traditional Λ(1405) resonance near 1405 MeV/c², or a higher-mass Λ*(1420)-like state associated with a two-pole structure, and what Σπ invariant-mass measurements can decisively determine its mass, width, and pole structure?

evidence.quote: This topic is related to a new puzzle in the physics of kaon-nucleon interaction: the nature of the Λ(1405) - single or double pole structure?

It is urgently important to distinguish the Λ∗ mass, 1405 or 1420 MeV/c2. A bubble-chamber Σπ invariant-mass data from stopped K− on 4He supports the Λ(1405) Ansatz [6]. A stopped K− on D experiment [7] would provide a decisive datum for the mass discrimination.
Where is the position of the I = 0 L = 0 K−p quasi-bound state? This question is directly connected to the strength of the s-wave I = 0 K¯N interaction.

accepted.question_text: Do antikaon-mediated kaonic nuclear bound states, especially systems such as K−pp, exist as discrete observable states with large binding energies and measurable decay widths, or are antikaon-nuclear systems only weakly bound and very short-lived; if such states exist, what production mechanisms, binding energies, and decay widths consistently describe observations from stopped-K−, proton-induced, and antiproton-absorption reactions?
accepted.context_brief: Existence and properties of kaonic nuclei

evidence.quote: It was originally suggested that in the few-body nuclear systems the (strongly attractive) isospin I = 0 K¯N interaction can favour the formation of discrete and narrow barK-nuclear bound states with large binding energy (100 MeV or even more). Recent theoretical works suggest, however, that such deeply bound kaonic nuclear states do not exist: antikaon-nuclear systems might only weakly bound and very short-lived. Different interpretations for the existing experimental results are given

Many questions about kaonic nuclei are still open: production mechanism, binding energy, decay widths etc. Experimental data claim the observation of kaonic nuclei in different reactions using stopped K−, proton-induced reaction or antiproton absorption [6,7]. However, the overall picture is not coherent since the binding energies and decay width extracted from data with different production reactions vary in a broad range.

While unambiguous conclusions about quasibound antikaon-nuclear systems can at present not yet be drawn, further progress is expected to come from detailed investigations of exclusive final states following K− absorption and photon- or hadron-induced K+ production on nuclei

a dedicated search is planned to look for an experimental proof of the existence of antikaon-mediated deeply bound nuclear systems [2]. If they exist, antikaon bound nuclear states (K¯-nuclear clusters) will indeed offer ideal conditions

accepted.question_text: What real and imaginary K−p scattering lengths, K−n scattering information, and isospin-dependent antikaon-nucleon scattering lengths are consistent with kaonic hydrogen and kaonic deuterium measurements, low-energy K−p data, and πΣ mass spectra, and how should those data constrain subthreshold antikaon-nucleon interaction amplitudes used in kaonic-nucleus calculations?

evidence.quote: The kaonic hydrogen was measured by the DEAR Collaboration (on DAΦNE) with an unprecedented precision, leading to a lively debate on the kaon-proton scattering length extraction procedure, and on the compatibility with existent kaon-nucleon scattering data.

the corresponding observables of kaonic deuterium are a hot topic since they are necessary to extract the isospin dependent K−-nucleon scattering lengths. For the first time kaonic deuterium was studied by SIDDHARTA very recently. The extraction of the scattering lengths is subject of intense theoretical work
The K−p scattering lengths deduced from these measurements are not fully consistent: a(K−p) = −0.47 (±0.10) + i 0.30 (±0.17) [fm] [DEAR] and a(K−p) = −0.78 (±0.18) + i 0.49 (±0.37) [fm] [KEK].
With systematic experiments one can extract the K−N scattering amplitudes below the K−N threshold down to about -35 MeV. At this moment one has only K1H [1] and K4He [2] data.

accepted.question_text: How sensitive are kaonic atom observables to nuclear density and to the nuclear interior, and can the deep phenomenological K−-nucleus optical potentials with real-part depths around 180 MeV at nuclear-matter density be reconciled with chiral-motivated potentials whose corresponding depths are only about 30–40 MeV?

evidence.quote: The expression ‘kaonic atoms puzzle’ refers to an apparent conflict between phenomenological optical potentials obtained from fits to kaonic atom data and the corresponding potentials constructed from more fundamental approaches [1,2]. Whereas the best-fit phenomenological potentials have for the real part typical depths of 180 MeV at nuclear-matter densities, the corresponding depth of chiral-motivated potentials [3] is 30-40 MeV.
The question of how sensitive kaonic atom observables are to the nuclear density was discussed recently in terms of a functional derivative approach [4].
The question of how sensitive kaonic atoms are to the interior of nuclei is re-investigated here by analysing kaonic atoms in parallel with antiprotonic atoms and scattering of low energy p¯.

accepted.question_text: What is the absorption-dependent, imaginary part of the K− nuclear potential in normal nuclear matter, and how can pion-induced φ-meson and K− production measurements separate intrinsic in-medium φ-meson modifications from K− absorption behavior in nuclei?

evidence.quote: strangeness production in pion-induced reactions is well suited to study the kaon absorption in normal nuclear matter density.

On the other hand, in order to disentangle the intrinsic properties of the φ meson in the nucleus from the K− behavior, exclusive analysis can be carried out to tag the K− not coming from the φ decay.

The K− scattering length is known from kaonic atom experiments [2], while not very much is known on the absorption potential. The planned measurement should provide a valid contribution to determine the imaginary part of this potential.

accepted.question_text: What collision de-excitation cross sections and cascade-dynamics model are needed for kaonic hydrogen and kaonic deuterium so that X-ray yields, density dependence, nuclear absorption, Stark mixing, and strong-interaction widths can be interpreted accurately in experiments such as DEAR and SIDDHARTA?

evidence.quote: The interpretation of experimental data and planning the high precision measurements [1] of the X-ray yields in the kaonic hydrogen pK− and deuterium dK− require an additional theoretical study of cascade processes in such atoms.

The attempts to create a universal code based on pure quantum mechanical calculating the cascade characteristics encounter the problem of the lack of a complete set of the collision de-excitation cross-sections
We have analyzed our results to clear the answer of some important questions about the kaonic cascade dynamics.

We suggest that the SIDDHARTA experiment for K−d and K−p atoms are done in different density. Because if it is possible, We can take Γ2p as a free parameter then it can be determined more precisely by fitting the simulated x-ray curves with experimental results.

accepted.question_text: For reported structures in Λp, ppπ−, and related invariant-mass spectra from experiments such as E549, FINUDA, OBELIX, FOPI, and older K−d bubble-chamber observations, are the peaks evidence for Bound Kaonic Systems, or can they instead be explained by conventional mechanisms such as threshold cusp effects, two-nucleon absorption, ΣN conversion, or other final-state effects?

evidence.quote: It might be useful to point out at possible similarities of possible Bound Kaonic Systems (BKS) observations reported at this Workshop and performed in different experimental environments, as a start for a thorough understanding of a few disagreements among some of them.
For this structure both the interpretation of BKS or of threshold effect can in principle be suggested.

the signal was indicated to be due to a cusp effect related to the opening of the Σ0nπ− channel, rather than to a new resonance. Also in this case an alternative interpretation of the recently observed signal can be suggested.

accepted.question_text: Can kaon condensation occur in strong-interaction self-bound nuclear matter, with K− mesons serving as relevant degrees of freedom of self-bound strange matter, and can multi-antikaon hypernuclear configurations reach the roughly 320 MeV antikaon separation-energy threshold needed for conversion Λ → K¯N in matter?
accepted.context_brief: Kaon condensation in self-bound strange matter

evidence.quote: We focus on the question whether or not kaon condensation could occur in strong interaction self-bound nuclear matter, thus whether the K− mesons could be the relevant degrees of freedom of self-bound strange matter
This scenario requires that K¯ separation energy exceeds the threshold value of roughly mK + µN − mΛ ≈ 320 MeV, thus allowing for the conversion Λ → K¯N in matter.

in all cases the BK− does not exceed 120 MeV in these multistrange configurations, which is considerably short of the threshold value of ≈ 320 MeV necessary for the onset of kaon condensation under laboratory conditions.

accepted.question_text: Can stopped antiproton annihilation in light nuclei produce deeply bound double-strange, S = −2, double-antikaon dibaryon systems such as K−K−pp, and can exclusive measurements of K+K0 missing mass and correlated ΛΛ decays establish such states with sufficient resolution and statistics?

evidence.quote: Recently antiproton annihilation in nuclei was proposed to search for deeply bound double-strange systems with S = -2 of light nuclei [1, 2].
So there is reason to believe that one can produce S = -2 di-baryon systems with still higher binding energies and densities using antiproton annihilation at rest.
In this contribution we present details of experimental approaches to search for the most elementary S = -2 di-proton system using the antiproton annihilation reaction on 3He targets at rest

accepted.question_text: In hadron physics, how are hadron masses generated, how do hadron interactions change inside nuclear matter, and what is the structure of cold dense hadronic matter, as probed by low-energy antikaon-nucleus and antikaon-nucleon interactions?

evidence.quote: The scientific case of AMADEUS deals with one of the most important, yet unsolved, problems in hadron physics: how the hadron masses are generated, how the hadron interactions change in the nuclear medium and what is the structure of cold dense hadronic matter.
With AMADEUS these problems will be attacked by detailed studies of the antikaon nucleus/nucleon interaction at low-energy

accepted.question_text: Was the historical kaonic helium puzzle—the five-sigma discrepancy between theoretical expectations of an approximately zero eV strong-interaction shift for the kaonic helium-4 2p state and older measurements averaging about −43 eV—resolved by newer E570 and SIDDHARTA measurements showing a shift consistent with 0 eV?

evidence.quote: Prior to the experiment by the E570 group, the average of the three previous results was −43 ± 8 eV [3], while most of the theoretical calculations give ∼0 eV [2]. This five-sigma discrepancy between theory and experiment was known as the ‘kaonic helium puzzle.’ A resolution of this long-standing puzzle provided by the E570 group is now firmly established by the present work.
A new value of the strong interaction shift of the kaonic helium-4 2p state was determined to be 0 ± 6 (stat) ± 2 (syst) eV [1].
